case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: The filter caused harm without any third-party content doing the work. Where the injury runs through generated words rather than a feature's mechanics, courts still have to decide whether the design frame or the speech frame controls.
case.holding: Section 230 did not bar a negligent-design claim against Snapchat for its speed filter, because the claim faulted the design of the product itself rather than treating Snap as the publisher of any user's content.
case.why_ai_cites_it: The road around Zeran. Plaintiffs suing AI companies over harmful system behaviour plead design defect precisely because Lemmon holds that a duty to design reasonably exists independent of publishing, which is why current chatbot cases are framed as defective products rather than harmful speech.

reading.body:
Lemmon v. Snap, a 2021 case holding that a negligent-design claim against a social media feature was not barred by Section 230 because it faulted the product's design rather than any user's content, is cited by plaintiffs in the same four Character Technologies lawsuits as Twitter v. Taamneh and Winter v. Putnam.

That three different precedents recur across the identical four cases shows both sides in this specific litigation are arguing over which legal frame controls, design defect, information product, or platform speech, rather than disputing the facts themselves. The case's own stated limit is that the harm there ran through a feature's mechanics with no third-party content involved, while an AI chatbot's harm runs through generated words, leaving open which frame, design or speech, actually controls when the harm comes from what the system said rather than what it did.

The data does not say which frame has prevailed in any of the four cases, only that this precedent is the plaintiffs' vehicle for arguing the design frame should control.

section.name: AI Case Law: The Precedents Behind the Defenses
